Spotting Hidden Anxiety as Term One Winds Down

By the end of Term One, many Brisbane kids are exhausted. Routines have shifted, homework has picked up, and there can be more tests, projects, and after-school activities. It can all feel like a lot, even for kids who usually cope well.

Anxiety in children does not always look like obvious worry or panic. It often hides behind everyday things like tummy aches, grumpy outbursts, or being “too tired” for school. As the term wraps up, transitions, social changes, and pressure about schoolwork can bring that hidden anxiety closer to the surface. When we know what to look for, we can notice the signs early and get support from a child psychologist in Brisbane before things build up.

Subtle Signs Your Child Is Not Just “Tired”

A tired child at the end of term is very normal. The tricky part is telling the difference between normal fatigue and anxiety that needs extra care. Some physical signs of anxiety can be easy to miss, such as tummy aches or headaches that keep coming back (especially on school mornings), trouble falling asleep, frequent nightmares or waking in the night, changes in appetite, and seeming run down or “unwell” without a clear cause.

Behaviour changes can also be a clue, and parents often describe these as moodiness or attitude. You might notice clinginess at school drop-off, even if they were fine earlier in the term, irritability or snapping at family after school, or tears over small problems like a missing pencil or a change in plans. Anxiety can also show up as perfectionism with homework, needing things to be “just right” and getting upset with small mistakes, or as a sudden refusal to join activities they usually enjoy, such as sports or music.

School-related hints can tell us a lot, too. This might look like more arguments or complaints about going to school, asking to stay home with vague reasons like “I feel funny,” comments about friends being mean, leaving them out, or changing groups, or teachers mentioning that your child seems distracted, unusually quiet, or not like themselves.

Normal end-of-term tiredness usually eases with a relaxed weekend or a few quieter days. Anxiety is more likely when:

  • The signs keep going for weeks
  • Things slowly get worse instead of better
  • School, friendships, or family life are clearly affected

If you are unsure, trust your gut. You know your child’s usual patterns. A child psychologist in Brisbane can help you sort out what is typical stress and what might be anxiety.

What Makes Brisbane Kids Anxious at Term’s End

Different children worry about different things, but we see some common themes as Term One edges towards holidays. Academic pressures often build up, including NAPLAN practice for some year levels, upcoming tests, projects or class presentations, fear of getting things wrong or letting the teacher down, and worry about what school reports might say.

Social stress can be just as strong as schoolwork stress. For some children, it is the ongoing uncertainty and change, friendship reshuffles as groups form and change, playground conflicts or feeling left out at lunch or sport, anxiety about camps, excursions, sport trials or performances, or not knowing who to sit with or partner with in class.

There are also local lifestyle factors that can add to the load. These can include busy afternoons filled with sport, music, and tutoring, long drives in Brisbane traffic between school, home, and activities, warm, sticky evenings that make it harder to sleep well, and the quiet pressure kids feel to “keep up” with siblings or classmates.

Often, children keep their biggest worries to themselves. They may not say, “I am scared of disappointing you,” but you might notice:

  • They ask lots of checking questions about how you feel about their results
  • They compare their work to others and seem upset if they are not “the best”
  • They worry about something bad happening when you are not with them

When we understand what might be feeding the anxiety, we are in a better position to respond calmly and kindly.

How Parents Can Gently Support Anxious Kids

You do not have to fix everything overnight. Small, steady changes at home can make your child feel safer and more settled.

Start with a calm after-school routine. Many kids hold it together all day, then fall apart once they are home. It can help to:

  • Offer a drink and snack as soon as they walk in
  • Give them 20 to 30 minutes of quiet time before homework or big chats
  • Keep screens calm and predictable, rather than high drama right away
  • Avoid grilling them about their day the moment they get in the car

The way we talk about worries can either soothe or stir things up. Try to:

  • Name feelings gently: “I wonder if you felt a bit nervous about that test?”
  • Validate their experience: “That sounds hard, no wonder you were upset.”
  • Avoid comments like “Don’t be silly” or “You’re fine”, even when meant kindly

Simple tools can help kids feel they have some control, including slow belly breathing (such as counting to four on the breath in and out), grounding activities like noticing 5 things they can see or 3 things they can hear, predictable morning and bedtime routines, and visual planners for the week so they can see what is coming up.

Working with the school often makes a big difference. You might:

  • Ask the teacher for a quick chat or email update
  • Share a few key things your child is finding hard
  • Discuss small supports, like where your child sits, extra time to prepare for speaking in front of the class, or quiet check-ins during the day

When school and home give the same calm message, children feel more secure.

When to Consider Seeing a Child Psychologist in Brisbane

Some anxiety is part of growing up. However, there are times when extra help is important. Red flags can include:

  • Anxiety that has been strong and steady for more than a month
  • Big meltdowns or panic-like symptoms around going to school
  • Harsh self-talk, like calling themselves “stupid” or “a failure”
  • Pulling back from friends or avoiding activities they once enjoyed

A child psychologist in Brisbane can support your child with evidence-based approaches like cognitive-behaviour strategies and play-based work. The focus is on building skills, confidence, and a shared language for feelings so your child feels less alone and more capable.

At Michelle Barratt Psychology, we use a warm, family-centred approach. Parents and carers are involved, and we work alongside schools where helpful. Strategies are tailored to your child’s age, personality, and strengths, whether sessions are in Toowong, Wynnum West, or through Telehealth.

Seeking support is not overreacting. Early help often means fewer struggles in later terms and school years. It can also bring relief to you as a parent, knowing you are not carrying this on your own.

Taking Calm Next Steps Before Term Two Begins

The school holidays are a good time to slow the pace and pay gentle attention to how your child is really doing. You do not need big, dramatic changes. Small steps can shift the tone at home.

You might:

  • Plan some simple, calm family time without rushing
  • Review after-school activities and consider dropping one if things feel too full
  • Have open chats with your child about what feels hard or worrying at school
  • Touch base with their teacher if you are noticing ongoing changes

If you are concerned about hidden anxiety, professional guidance from Michelle Barratt Psychology can help you feel clearer and more confident. With the right support, Brisbane kids can head into Term Two feeling more secure, and parents can feel steadier about how to help them handle life at school and at home.
